chapter: Los Angeles, Ellington and the recording scene
title: Duke's offers to join, sitting in without a bass book, and working with Parker
summary: He turned Duke down two or three times, sat in at the Oasis where there was no bass part, and counts Charlie Parker and Lester sessions among his priceless moments.

story.theme_name: Duke Ellington and his orchestra, as others knew them
story.community_name: Duke Ellington: the band, the man, his men

blocks.x: He asked you more than one time to join the band, right?
How many times? Do you remember?

Oh, it was maybe two or three times, whenever he'd have a bass problem. But the fact that he thought enough of me to want me in his band really satisfied my ego, because he might have let me play the tuba and do the things I wanted to do, but I didn't think there was much of a chance for me to do much writing for Duke Ellington. So I stuck to my guns. I have no regrets. Just the fact that he wanted me was enough.
You sat in with the band a few times.
I remember, I think, at the Oasis you...
At the Oasis, when Wendell Marshall... Yeah, I sat in with the band. And the funny thing about that band, there was no bass book, you know...
That was true of several chairs.
Yeah. [LAUGHS] I'd say, "Where's the music?" He'd say, "Oh, you'll hear it."
Even when Wendell was there, there was no bass book, right?

Well, a smattering of a book. But things like "Cottontail" and "Perdido" and "Caravan" and those kind of things, stuff where you think there would be a part, there was no part. So he'd start, and I'd just play what I heard.
Oh, it was fun, yeah. Those were some of the priceless moments in life that you can't... I don't think I've ever talked about it before. But that was one of the priceless ones.

And I have to say a few others were, like, working with Charlie Parker. I made a lot of records with him on Dial. It's funny... And I made records with Lester, too. But with these guys, I knew that here was something special that would live forever, you know. You could realize it at the time, that, "Hey, I'm fortunate to be here."
